title: A story with a twist
job: A six-sentence narrative with a line of dialogue inside it
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: SIX SENTENCES, AND ALMOST NO NEW VOCABULARY. L3-M10's account was eight and this is six, because a twist needs less room than a day. inquit, inquam, subitō and venī are the only fresh rows the narrative needs; everything else is in the index already, including M8's imperfect for the background and M9's places.

THE TWO PAST TENSES FINALLY DIVIDE THE WORK, AND THAT IS WHAT THE IMPERFECT WAS DEFERRED FOR. Background goes in the imperfect — ōlim Rōmae habitābam, cotīdiē ībam, aeger eram — and events go in the perfect — subitō Mārcus vēnit, postrēmō domum īvī. L2-M10 and L3-M10 both had to recast a state as an event because no imperfect existed, and a story with only perfects reads as a list of unconnected facts. S10's mistake plate is exactly that sentence.

subitō MARKS THE TURN AND THE TENSE DOES THE WORK. A narrative changes gear by changing tense, not by adding a word — so subitō only tells you the event was quick, and an imperfect after it is still background (S08: the state itself changed suddenly). S03's plate is an imperfect where the first event belongs, which is the reflex after two sentences of background.

PRO-DROP AND ITS ONE EXCEPTION, AT SIX SENTENCES: the subject is named exactly ONCE, at the sentence where it changes. Mārcus arrives and is named; nothing before or after him is. L2-M10 set this rule at four sentences and L3-M10 held it at eight; a narrative with two people in it needs the name at precisely the clause that changes hands and nowhere else.

inquit IS POSTPOSITIVE AND THAT IS THIS MODULE'S ONE HARD FACT. It means 'he says' AND 'he said' — the same shape for both, like M6's solvit — and it goes AFTER the first word or two of the quotation: "Venī", inquit, "domum". English puts 'he said' outside the line and Latin puts it inside, splitting the quotation around it. An author who writes inquit first has produced something no Roman wrote. A short quoted question counts as one unit, so inquit follows the whole of it — the rule is about never being FIRST rather than about a precise slot. inquam is its I-shape and behaves the same way.

DIRECT SPEECH IS THE OPPOSITE OF L3-M5's REPORTED SPEECH, AND BOTH ARE NOW YOURS. dīxit sē venīre reports without quoting and has no word for 'that'; "Venī", inquit quotes what was actually said. This module writes one of each so the contrast is visible — what somebody said, and what you say they said.

sentences.cue: I used to live at Rome.

words.note: 'Once, back then'. M8's word, and the opening of any story: it marks a stretch rather than a moment.
'At Rome' — M9's locative, with no preposition.
'I used to live' — M8's imperfect of habitō. Background, not event: a narrative sets its scene in this tense.

sentences.trap: A story opens in the IMPERFECT, and until M8 this course could not do it. L2-M10 and L3-M10 both had to recast a state as an event because no imperfect existed; now background goes in one tense and events in another, which is what Latin narrative actually does.
sentences.sound: Ō-lim RŌ-mae ha-bi-TĀ-bam. Nine syllables and three long vowels.

sentences.cue: Every day I used to go to the office.

words.note: 'Every day'. L1-M4's word, and it takes no ending.
'To', with the object shape after it — required, because an office is not a city.
'Office' after ad. L3-M8's word.
'I used to go' — M8's imperfect of eō: eō, ībam, īvī.

sentences.trap: More background, and no subject named. The first sentence established who and this one carries nothing but the habit — which is L2-M10's pro-drop rule at the front of a story rather than in the middle of one.

words.note: 'Suddenly'. It takes no ending and it goes at the front, which is where a narrative wants it.
A Roman man's name in the subject shape. He is named because the subject has CHANGED, which is the one place a narrative must put it back.
'He came' — the perfect of veniō, and one bar from venit, 'he comes'. The first EVENT of the story, after two sentences of background.

sentences.trap: The tense changes and the story starts. Two imperfects have set a scene and this perfect is the first thing that happens in it — so the twist of a narrative is marked by a tense rather than by a word, and subitō only tells you it was quick.
sentences.sound: SU-bi-tō MĀR-cus VĒ-nit. Seven syllables, and the long ō of subitō is where the story turns.

variations.changed: subitō dropped, which makes it ordinary

mistake.why: an imperfect for an event. It would say Marcus was in the middle of coming, which is background rather than a turn — and after two sentences of imperfects the tense is the reflex, which is exactly why this is the plate.

sentences.usage: Said at the moment a story starts.
sentences.mnemonic: A perfect is where the story turns.

words.note: 'Come!' — veniō's order shape. L1-M5 named this key thirty-nine modules ago and no module has written it until now.
'He says' and 'he said' — the same shape for both, like M6's solvit. It goes AFTER the first word or two of a quotation, never before it.
'Home' — the to-shape, with no preposition. L2-M4's word, and M9's closed list.

sentences.trap: inquit goes INSIDE the quotation, after its first word. English puts 'he said' before or after the whole line and Latin puts it in the middle — so the quotation is split around the reporting verb, and an author who writes inquit first has produced something no Roman wrote.
sentences.sound: VE-nī, IN-quit, DO-mum. Six syllables, and inquit is the unstressed middle of the line.

variations.cue: "Come to Rome", he said.
variations.changed: M9's city as the destination

variations.cue: "Home", he said, "come".
variations.changed: the two halves of the quotation swapped

variations.cue: He said I was coming home.
variations.changed: L3-M5's reported speech, which quotes nobody

mistake.why: inquit in front of the quotation. It is postpositive and there is no version of the sentence where it opens one — English's order is the error, and it is the only hard fact this module has.

sentences.cue: I was ill; so I did not go.

words.note: 'Ill' — aeger, aegra, aegrum. L3-M7's word.
'I was' — M8's imperfect of sum, the state that went on. Every module from L1-M9 to L3-M10 said fuī here because there was nothing else.
'And so'. L1-M9's word, first in its clause — the consequence pointing back.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'I went' — the perfect of eō. An event, against the state in the first half.

sentences.trap: Both tenses in one sentence and each doing its own job. eram is the state I was in and īvī is the thing that did not happen — and this is the division the whole course waited thirty-four modules for, working inside a five-word clause pair.

variations.cue: I was ill; so I did not go.
variations.changed: spoken by a woman

variations.cue: I was ill; so I was at home.
variations.changed: M9's locative, and both halves imperfect

variations.cue: I was ill; so I did not go.
variations.changed: the perfect of sum, which treats the illness as an event

sentences.usage: Said explaining why you missed something.

sentences.cue: "Why did you not come?", he said.

words.note: 'Why'. L1-M9's question word, and the one that asks for a cause — quia and ideō answer it.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'You came' — the perfect's you-shape, -istī where the present is -īs. L2-M8's errāvistī was the same ending.
'He says' and 'he said' — the same shape for both, like M6's solvit. It goes AFTER the first word or two of a quotation, never before it.

sentences.trap: Here inquit comes after the whole quotation, because the quotation is a question and splitting it would break it. The rule is 'after the first word or two' and a short question counts as one unit — so the constraint is about not putting inquit FIRST rather than about where exactly it lands.
sentences.sound: CŪR nōn vē-NIS-tī, IN-quit. Seven syllables and two long vowels, both in the question.

variations.cue: "Why did you not come?", said Marcus.
variations.changed: the speaker named after the verb, which is the usual order

variations.cue: "When did you come?", he said.
variations.changed: L2-M6's question word

variations.cue: "Why are you not coming?", he said.
variations.changed: the present inside the quotation

words.note: 'Ill' — aeger, aegra, aegrum.
'I say, I said' — inquit's I-shape, and it is postpositive too. inquam, inquit: the only two shapes of this verb this course writes.
'I was' — M8's imperfect of sum.

sentences.trap: A quotation split around inquam, and the quotation is two words with the verb of the story between them. That is as compressed as this construction gets — and it is the shape a Roman used constantly, because the reporting verb is unstressed and belongs where nobody would look for it.

sentences.cue: Suddenly I was no longer ill.

words.note: 'Suddenly'. It takes no ending and it goes at the front, which is where a narrative wants it.
'Not' — and nōn iam together mean 'no longer'. M6's pair.
'Already' — and with nōn in front it is 'no longer'. M6's word, built from two the course already had.
'Ill' — aeger, aegra, aegrum.
'I was' — M8's imperfect of sum, and here it is the twist: the state changed.

sentences.trap: An imperfect with subitō in front of it, which looks like the plate on S03 and is not. There the imperfect would have been an event; here the state itself is what changed suddenly — so a state can turn abruptly, and the tense still holds it.
sentences.sound: SU-bi-tō nōn I-am AE-ger E-ram. Nine syllables, and the long ō is the turn.

sentences.cue: "Come to Rome", he said; so I went.

words.note: 'Come!' — veniō's order shape, and a key L1-M5 held free for thirty-nine modules.
'He says' and 'he said' — the same shape for both, like M6's solvit. It goes AFTER the first word or two of a quotation, never before it.
'To Rome' — M9's city, with no preposition.
'And so'. L1-M9's word, first in its clause.
'I went' — the perfect of eō. The event the quotation caused.

sentences.trap: A quotation, a consequence and an event in five words. The reported line is what somebody actually said and the perfect after it is what it caused — so direct speech does inside a story what L3-M5's reported speech does in a conversation, and both are now in the learner's hands.
sentences.sound: VE-nī, IN-quit, RŌ-mam; I-ta-que Ī-vī. Eleven syllables and four long vowels.

variations.cue: He said I was coming to Rome.
variations.changed: L3-M5's reported speech, which quotes nobody and names no words

sentences.usage: Said telling what someone said and what you did.

sentences.cue: I used to live at Rome; every day I went to the office; suddenly Marcus came; "Come home", he said; I was ill; finally I went home.

words.note: 'Once, back then'. M8's word, opening the story.
'At Rome' — M9's locative.
'I used to live' — M8's imperfect: background.
'Every day'. L1-M4's word.
'I used to go' — M8's imperfect of eō: more background.
'Suddenly'. It takes no ending and it goes at the front, which is where a narrative wants it.
A Roman man's name in the subject shape, named because the subject changed.
'He came' — the perfect of veniō: the first event.
'Come!' — veniō's order shape, inside the quotation.
'He says' and 'he said' — the same shape for both, like M6's solvit. It goes AFTER the first word or two of a quotation, never before it.
'Home' — the to-shape, with no preposition.
'I was' — M8's imperfect of sum: the state behind the decision.
'Finally'. L2-M10's closer — after it a listener expects you to stop.
'I went' — the perfect of eō: the last event.

sentences.trap: Six clauses, two tenses dividing the work, one quotation with the verb inside it, and the subject named exactly once — at the sentence where it changed. That is a narrative rather than an account, and the difference from L3-M10's eight sentences is that this one has a tense for its background and a line of somebody's actual words in it.
sentences.sound: Thirty-seven syllables — the longest line in the course. Read it in six pieces, one per clause, and the two tenses will separate themselves.

mistake.display: Ōlim Rōmae habitāvī; cotīdiē ad officīnam īvī; subitō Mārcus vēniēbat.
mistake.why: every tense exactly backwards: perfects for the background and an imperfect for the event. It is the sentence this whole course would have had to write before M8, and it reads as a list of three unconnected facts rather than a story — which is what the imperfect was deferred thirty-four modules to prevent.

sentences.usage: Said telling a story with a turn in it.
sentences.mnemonic: Two tenses, one quotation, one named subject.
